claims.text: Multi-principal-element alloying induces severe lattice distortion in refractory single-phase BCC alloys.
Severe lattice distortion generates wavy edge-dislocation lines.
Wavy edge-dislocation lines reduce dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
The initial refractory high-entropy alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
The initial alloy is prepared by arc melting and homogenization.
Changing atomic-radius mismatch through composition changes the extent of lattice distortion.
A controlled comparison can vary lattice distortion while maintaining similar grain size and phase purity.
Relevant high-temperature testing spans 500°C to 900°C at a controlled low strain rate comparable to in situ neutron-diffraction testing.
Lattice distortions displace edge-dislocation cores from their neutral planes.
Displacement of edge-dislocation cores from their neutral planes causes wavy dislocation configurations.
Reduced dislocation mobility helps maintain ductility at high temperature.
Reduced dislocation mobility improves toughness at high temperature.
Increasing lattice distortion will reduce the loss of yield strength at elevated temperature relative to a low-distortion baseline.
Increasing lattice distortion will increase elevated-temperature plastic-strain capacity relative to a low-distortion baseline.
Increasing lattice distortion will increase elevated-temperature toughness relative to a low-distortion baseline.
Less compositional variation produces lower lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase refractory BCC HEAs between roughly 500°C and 900°C at relatively low strain rates.
The proposed mechanism may fail in multiphase materials or at extremely high strain rates because other mechanisms may dominate.
